SO-101 and LeRobot: first steps

The SO-101 is an open robot arm by The Robot Studio and Hugging Face. LeRobot is the Python library you use to set it up, control it and teach it tasks from demonstrations. This guide summarises the official procedure and adds a virtual-arm practice run to every step.

The official LeRobot documentation is authoritative. Commands change between library versions; this page reflects them as of 29 October 2026. Where anything differs, follow the current guide on huggingface.co.

  1. What you need
  2. Installation

  4. Servo IDs

01 — What you need

Two arms, six servos each

The setup has two arms. You guide the leader arm with your own hand and the follower arm repeats the movement. Both use six Feetech STS3215 servos. The follower uses 1:345 gearing throughout; the leader has different ratios on different joints (1:191, 1:345 and 1:147) so it is easy to move by hand. The exact table is in the official guide.1

You also need a servo driver board for each arm, USB cables, a power supply that matches your servo variant, and a computer with Python. The full bill of materials and print files are in the project repository.2 The build from printing to first motion is covered in SO-101 assembly, step by step.

Before you buy anything, try the arm in the SO-101 simulation. You’ll see how the joints move and what the arm can do.

02 — Installation

Python 3.12 and LeRobot

LeRobot requires Python 3.12 or newer.3 All our SO-101 guides use the same install from PyPI, pinned to version 0.6.1, which we tested against the virtual arm; Feetech servo support is included:1

python3.12 -m venv .venv-lerobot
source .venv-lerobot/bin/activate
pip install "lerobot[feetech,core-scripts]==0.6.1"

Windows: py -3.12 -m venv .venv-lerobot and .venv-lerobot\Scripts\activate. The official guide recommends a conda environment (Miniforge) and installing from git; the same pip install works inside a conda environment. ffmpeg is needed for video in datasets (recording with cameras): Linux sudo apt install ffmpeg, macOS brew install ffmpeg, conda conda install ffmpeg -c conda-forge.3

03 — Port

Find each arm’s port

lerobot-find-port asks you to unplug the USB cable and prints the port that disappeared. On Linux it looks like /dev/ttyACM0, on macOS /dev/tty.usbmodem…, on Windows COM3. Repeat for both arms. On Linux you may need to grant access to the port, for example sudo chmod 666 /dev/ttyACM0.1

Dry run: dry-run servo setup, step 1. The virtual arm connects without a cable.

04 — Servo IDs

Each servo gets its own ID

New servos all ship with the same ID, so on a shared bus they would talk over each other. lerobot-setup-motors walks you through it: only one servo is connected to the board at a time, starting with the gripper (ID 6) and ending with the base (ID 1).1

lerobot-setup-motors \
    --robot.type=so101_follower \
    --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0

The leader arm is the same, with --teleop.type=so101_leader and --teleop.port=….

Dry run: the wizard, step 2. The six emulated STS3215 servos all have ID 1 “out of the box”, just like real ones.

05 — Calibration

The centre and range of every joint

lerobot-calibrate first records the middle of the range (all joints centred, as in the picture in the guide), then you move each joint from stop to stop.1 Give the arms fixed names in --robot.id and --teleop.id: LeRobot stores the calibration under that ID, and you use the same ID for teleoperation and recording.4

lerobot-calibrate \
    --robot.type=so101_follower \
    --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 \
    --robot.id=my_follower_arm

Dry run: the wizard, step 3. You can download the virtual arm’s calibration as JSON and see what LeRobot stores. A real arm has to be calibrated on its own, though.

Careful: during calibration servo torque is off and the arm can drop. Hold it.

06 — Teleoperation

The follower repeats the leader

lerobot-teleoperate \
    --robot.type=so101_follower \
    --robot.port=/dev/ttyACM0 \
    --robot.id=my_follower_arm \
    --teleop.type=so101_leader \
    --teleop.port=/dev/ttyACM1 \
    --teleop.id=my_leader_arm

If a calibration is missing, the command runs it first, according to the guide.4

Safety: clamp the arm to the table, keep its reach clear and keep the power supply within reach. Kits are for ages 14 and up, younger children only under adult supervision.

Dry run: the wizard, step 4 (testing with sliders). Connecting a real arm straight from the browser stays hidden until it passes a safety review on hardware; drive the real arm through LeRobot.

07 — Learning from demos

Record, train, run

The next steps are in the guide “Getting started with real-world robots”: lerobot-record records demonstrations (joint movements and camera footage) into a dataset, and lerobot-train trains a model from them, for example ACT. The guide recommends starting with at least 50 episodes, about 10 per object position, with the cameras fixed in place.4 According to the guide, training takes several hours and expects a GPU (or Apple silicon).

You can try the principle in the simulation: the Learning from demonstration panel records your movement and the arm repeats it. The recordings can be converted into a LeRobot-format dataset on the LeRobot export page. They are joint positions only, with no camera footage, from a simplified simulation. They are not enough to train a model for a real arm; they help you understand the data format.

The exported dataset uses format v2.1. We have not yet checked whether the latest LeRobot reads it without conversion.

Next

Try the arm in the simulation and the servo setup in the dry-run wizard. What to buy and where is in the SO-101 buying plan, and the assembly guide takes you through the build. We sell nothing; we work from the project’s open documentation and the authors are not affiliated with us.
